414.title: Pleasant places (Psalm 16)
414.hook: the lines are fallen to me in pleasant places
414.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 16 in daily prayer, and some churches read it in the Easter season, following Peter's sermon in Acts 2, which hears it as a psalm of resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: enosh, small under the moon and stars, and yet remembered. Your line: what are we, that you care?

In the book of Joshua, the land is handed out by lot. A surveyor goes into the hills with a long cord, and the land is measured out with ropes: this field is yours, that slope is your cousin's. Where your lines fell, that was your share, your inheritance, for good. Some families got rich valley soil. Some got rocky hillsides. The priestly tribe of Levi got no land at all; God told them, I am your portion. And a psalm-writer, looking at his own life, uses that picture: the measuring lines have fallen for me. And he says where they fell.
screen: `A SURVEYOR WITH A CORD.` → `WHERE YOUR LINES FELL.` → `SOME GOT NO LAND AT ALL.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage." Just before that, he names what his share is: "The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup." Like the Levites, his real allotment isn't a field. It's God. The psalm is honest that this is a choice of attention, not a lucky break: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." Set: placed on purpose, like a photo on your desk where you'll see it. The result is joy, even in the body: my heart is glad, my flesh will rest in hope. Then the psalm reaches past death: you will not leave my soul in the grave. And it ends: "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore." Christians have heard that ending as resurrection. In the book of Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter quotes this psalm to the crowd and says it speaks of Jesus, whose body did not stay in the grave. One honest note. The heading calls it a michtam of David, and nobody is sure what michtam means. A golden poem, a secret, an inscription: scholars have guessed. The sources don't settle it. What the psalm does say is plain: wherever the lines fell, the LORD is the portion, and the heritage is goodly.
screen: `THE LORD IS MY PORTION.` · `I HAVE SET THE LORD BEFORE ME.` · `THE PATH OF LIFE, FULNESS OF JOY.` · `MICHTAM: NOBODY'S SURE.` · then, large: `THE LINES ARE FALLEN UNTO ME IN PLEASANT PLACES.`

segments.voice: Think of where your lines have fallen, and pick just one pleasant place: a kitchen where people laugh, a walk you take, a chair by a window. Picture its light and its sounds, and say quietly, this is mine, and it's good; if some of your lines fell on rocky ground, you don't have to pretend otherwise. If you pray, give thanks for it.
Pleasant places. In Psalm sixteen, where the measuring lines of a life have fallen, when God is its portion.
Your line: a goodly heritage. The Levites got no field, and still had a portion. Day four hundred fourteen.

415.title: The heavens declare (Psalm 19)
415.hook: the sky speaks without words, and the law is sweeter than honey
415.howItsDone: Many preachers say the last verse of Psalm 19 before a sermon, and Christians pray the psalm in daily prayer; Haydn's oratorio The Creation sets its opening as a chorus.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pleasant places, where the measuring lines of a life fall when God is its portion. Your line: a goodly heritage.

Sunrise doesn't make a sound. Neither does a sunset, or the moon coming up orange over a parking lot, or a thunderhead building on a summer afternoon. And yet people stop their cars for these things. They nudge whoever is next to them: look. Something is being said, and everyone seems to get it, in every language, without a word. A poet in ancient Israel noticed that too. And then, halfway through his poem, he made a turn that readers still talk about. He turned from the sky to a book.
screen: `SUNRISE MAKES NO SOUND.` → `EVERYONE SAYS: LOOK.` → `FROM THE SKY TO A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Psalm nineteen opens, in the King James Bible: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the message to the next, like a relay. Then a paradox. The King James reads, "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." But the Hebrew is even stranger. Literally: no speech, no words, their voice is not heard. And yet, the next verse says, their line has gone out through all the earth. The sky speaks without saying anything, and it's heard everywhere precisely because it uses no words. Then the sun comes out of its tent like a bridegroom, like a runner glad to run its course, and nothing is hidden from its heat. Then, the turn. Without warning, the poem moves from the sun to the law of the LORD, which is perfect, and restores the soul. Of God's judgments it says, "More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb." Why put the sky and the law in one poem? Many readers think that's the whole point. God speaks two ways: wordlessly, through everything that's made, and in words, through scripture. Joseph Haydn set the opening to music in his oratorio The Creation, and the psalm's last line is one many preachers still say before they begin: "Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer."

segments.voice: Look at the sky, through a window or outside, and don't name anything: not the cloud type, not the weather. Just watch the light, the color, how fast or slow things move, and let it say whatever it's saying without words. If you pray, bring one sentence back in, the psalm's last line: let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight.

416.title: My God, my God (Psalm 22)
416.hook: a cry of abandonment that turns to praise; Jesus prayed its first line on the cross
416.howItsDone: Some churches read Psalm 22 on Good Friday, and in some traditions the altar is stripped on Maundy Thursday while it is said or sung; Christians also pray its first line in times of grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the firmament, declaring God's glory without a word. Your line: day unto day, speech.

At a graveside. In an empty kitchen. In the small hours, when prayers seem to hit the ceiling and fall back down. People have said one sentence there, or wanted to. It's the opening of Psalm twenty-two, and today begins in the dark. It's famous not only for what it says, but for who said it, long after it was written, hanging on a Roman cross outside Jerusalem, near the end.
screen: `PRAYERS THAT HIT THE CEILING.` → `TODAY BEGINS IN THE DARK.` → `WHO SAID IT, ON A CROSS.`

segments.voice: The psalm begins, in the King James Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring. Not a polite complaint. A howl. And notice it still says my God, twice. Even the cry of abandonment is addressed to God; the psalmist shouts toward the One who seems absent. Then it gets physical: enemies like bulls and dogs, bones out of joint, a tongue stuck to the jaw. "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture." The Gospels tell the crucifixion with this psalm close by: the mocking crowd, the thirst, and the soldiers gambling for Jesus' clothes, which John's Gospel says fulfilled this very line. Matthew and Mark both record that near the end, Jesus cried out the first line: "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christians read that cry in more than one way. Some hear real anguish: Jesus entering the deepest human darkness, the feeling of being forsaken, so that no one is ever alone in it again. Others point out that quoting a psalm's first line could call the whole psalm to mind. And the whole psalm doesn't end in the dark. Around verse twenty-two it turns: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee." The cry becomes a song, and by the end the psalm reaches the ends of the earth and generations not yet born. Plenty of Christians hold both readings at once. The cry is real. And the psalm doesn't stop at the cry.
screen: `MY GOD, TWICE, EVEN IN THE DARK.` · `GARMENTS PARTED, LOTS CAST.` · `ELI, ELI, LAMA SABACHTHANI.` · `THE CRY TURNS TO PRAISE.` · then, large: `MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?`

segments.voice: If something in your life right now feels like abandonment, a loss, a silence, an unanswered prayer, let it come up without tidying it. If you pray, say the first line slowly and mean it: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Notice you're still saying my God. If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing honestly, without pretending it's fine, and rest.

417.title: Whom shall I fear? (Psalm 27)
417.hook: the Lord is my light; one thing I ask, to dwell in his house
417.howItsDone: Some Christians pray Psalm 27 in times of fear, and it appears in daily prayer; in Jewish practice it is recited daily from the start of the month of Elul through the autumn festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: My God, my God, a cry that still says my God and turns to praise. Your line: even he cried this.

One request. Not three wishes, not a list. One. It's harder than it sounds: health, safety for the people you love, a little more money, the scan coming back clear, the person who left coming back. Psalm twenty-seven is sung by someone surrounded: enemies closing in, an army camped around, false witnesses lining up, and he even imagines his own father and mother turning away. If anyone has a long list of requests, it's him. And then he says: I've asked for one thing. Only one.
screen: `IF YOU COULD ASK FOR ONE THING.` → `SURROUNDED, WITH A LONG LIST.` → `ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: Psalm twenty-seven opens, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" Two questions, and they're not quite rhetorical. The psalmist knows exactly whom he could fear, and names them: evildoers, a host encamped against him, war rising up. The fear is real. The questions are his way of standing up inside it. Then, the one thing: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple." Not rescue first. Not victory. Nearness: to live close to God, and to look at his beauty. Everything else, the psalm seems to say, follows from that one thing, or matters less without it. The fear doesn't vanish all at once. Halfway through, the psalm swings back to pleading: hide not thy face from me. Then a tender line: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up." And it ends not with a victory but with waiting: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD." Wait, twice. Two things worth knowing. Jewish custom adds Psalm twenty-seven to daily prayer in the weeks around the High Holy Days in the fall. And the first words in Latin, Dominus illuminatio mea, the Lord is my light, are the motto of the University of Oxford.
screen: `TWO QUESTIONS, ASKED INSIDE FEAR.` · `ONE THING: TO DWELL NEAR.` · `WHEN MY FATHER AND MOTHER FORSAKE ME.` · `WAIT, AND BE OF GOOD COURAGE.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS MY LIGHT; WHOM SHALL I FEAR?`

418.title: Joy in the morning (Psalm 30)
418.hook: weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning
418.howItsDone: Some churches read Psalm 30 in the Easter season, Christians pray it in times of recovery and thanksgiving, and its line 'joy cometh in the morning' is said at funerals and bedsides.

segments.voice: Yesterday: false witnesses closing in, and the LORD is my light. Your line: one thing I ask.

Three in the morning, wide awake. Lying there with a fever, or sitting in a waiting room as the clock crawls past three. The night after a breakup, or bad news, or a fight you can't take back. Things weigh more in the dark. Worries grow teeth. And then, sometimes without anything at all being fixed, the window goes gray, then pale, a bird starts up outside, and the same problem looks different in daylight. Not solved. Just survivable. Psalm thirty puts that whole stretch of night into a single line.
screen: `AWAKE PAST THREE.` → `WORRIES GROW TEETH IN THE DARK.` → `THEN THE WINDOW GOES GRAY.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty, in the King James Bible: "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." The Hebrew picture is even more vivid. The word for endure, yalin, means to lodge, to spend the night. Weeping comes in like an overnight guest. It's allowed in. It stays the night. But it doesn't move in. In the morning, joy arrives, and the guest leaves. The psalm is a thank-you, and it tells a story. When things were going well, the writer got comfortable: "In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved." Then God hid his face, he says, and he was troubled. He fell ill, or nearly died; he talks about going down to the pit. He cried out, and he was healed. Then the line about dancing: "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness." Sackcloth was the rough cloth people wore in grief. God, the psalm says, took it off him, like a parent changing a child's clothes, and dressed him in joy. The heading calls it a song at the dedication of the house, which the King James reads as the house of David; readers differ on which house is meant. In Jewish prayer books it's said each morning, and at Hanukkah, the feast of the temple's rededication. Some churches read it in the Easter season. The psalm doesn't say the night isn't real. It says the night isn't permanent.
screen: `WEEPING STAYS THE NIGHT, LIKE A GUEST.` · `I SAID, I SHALL NEVER BE MOVED.` · `MOURNING TURNED INTO DANCING.` · `THE NIGHT IS NOT PERMANENT.` · then, large: `WEEPING MAY ENDURE FOR A NIGHT.`

If you're in a long night now, you don't have to feel joy yet, just remember that mornings come, and if you pray, give thanks for one morning.

419.title: When I kept silent (Psalm 32)
419.hook: holding a wrong in, my bones wasted away; confessing, I was forgiven
419.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess in the sacrament of reconciliation; some Protestants confess privately to God or in prayers of confession in worship. Psalm 32 is one of the penitential psalms, prayed in Lent in some churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty: yalin, weeping stays the night like a guest, and your line, joy comes in the morning.

A sharp word to a friend, three weeks back. Credit taken for something that wasn't quite yours. A small lie, then another to cover it. Nobody found out. And yet it sits there, at night, in the shoulders, in the stomach. Something that small, held in, can get heavy. Long ago, someone wrote that weight down in a psalm that reads almost like a medical chart of a guilty conscience.
screen: `SOMETHING SMALL, NEVER SAID.` → `IT SITS IN THE SHOULDERS.` → `A CHART OF A GUILTY CONSCIENCE.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-two starts at the end of the story, with relief, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered." Then it goes back to tell how it got there. "When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer." Bones aging. Groaning all day. Dried out, like a field in August. The silence wasn't peaceful. It was exhausting. Then the turn, and it comes fast: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." I said I will confess, and you forgave. A weight carried for who knows how long lifts in a single breath. Then God speaks: "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye." And a gentle warning: don't be like a horse or a mule that has to be steered with a bit and bridle. Paul quotes its opening in his letter to the Romans. Western Christian tradition groups it with the penitential psalms, the psalms of turning back. Augustine's biographer says that as he was dying, Augustine had the penitential psalms copied and put on the wall where he could read them from his bed. Christians practice confession differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians confess to a priest in a sacrament. Some Protestants confess directly to God, some in a prayer said together in church, and some to a trusted friend, as the letter of James puts it: confess your faults one to another.

420.title: Taste and see (Psalm 34)
420.hook: O taste and see that the Lord is good
420.carry: near the brokenhearted, not the strong
420.howItsDone: Many churches, Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and others, sing 'O taste and see' during communion, a custom described as early as Cyril of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the penitential psalms: when I kept silence, my bones waxed old, and your line, silence was heavy.

You can read a whole cookbook about peaches: their varieties, their season, the chemistry of their sugars. You can become an expert. Then someone hands you a real one, warm from the tree, and you bite into it, and the juice runs down your wrist, and in two seconds you know something the whole book couldn't tell you. Some knowledge only comes through the mouth. One psalm turns that ordinary truth into an invitation, and it's been sung in churches for more than sixteen hundred years at one particular moment.
screen: `A WHOLE BOOK ABOUT PEACHES.` → `THEN A REAL ONE, WARM.` → `SOME KNOWLEDGE COMES BY MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-four, in the King James Bible: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Taste first, then see. Not see first, and maybe taste later if the evidence is good enough. The psalm puts experience before understanding: you come to know God's goodness the way you know a peach, by trying it. And this isn't a psalm of easy times. The heading ties it to David running for his life, pretending to be mad in front of a foreign king so he'd be let go. The heading names the king Abimelech, while the book of Samuel calls him Achish. Scholars have different explanations; the sources don't settle it. Either way, this is a song from someone who escaped by the skin of his teeth. "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears." And one of its best-known lines: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." Near the brokenhearted. Not the strong. The psalm is also an acrostic: in Hebrew, its verses run roughly through the alphabet, one letter after another, like a child's ABC of trust. And here's where the taste comes in for many Christians. In the fourth century, Cyril of Jerusalem described the newly baptized hearing a singer chant this verse as they came forward to receive communion: taste and see. Many churches still sing it at the Lord's table.
screen: `TASTE FIRST, THEN SEE.` · `A SONG OF A NARROW ESCAPE.` · `NIGH UNTO THE BROKEN HEART.` · `SUNG AT COMMUNION SINCE CYRIL.` · then, large: `O TASTE AND SEE THAT THE LORD IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one small bite or sip; if not, save this for your next meal. Don't chew yet: notice the texture and the temperature, then chew slowly and let the flavor arrive, change and fade. If you pray, give thanks for it.
Acrostic. A poem built so its verses run through the alphabet, one letter at a time, like this psalm of tasting God's goodness.
